extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical geometry / mathematical proofs (readers of Archimedes)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and interpret the stated postulates, propositions, and methods from Archimedes' treatises (On Spirals; On the Equilibrium of Planes). Focus is on the exact statements, relations, and the proof-methods (exhaustion, similar sectors, lever arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 1 (Equilibrium of equal weights at equal distances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal weights at equal distances are in equilibrium, and equal weights at unequal distances are not in equilibrium but incline towards the weight which is at the greater distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is taken as a fundamental axiom for subsequent balance/lever arguments; used to deduce unequal-weight and unequal-distance relations by subtraction/addition of weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 2 (Adding to a balanced weight disturbs equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, when weights at certain distances are in equilibrium, something be added to one of the weights, they are not in equilibrium but incline towards that weight to which the addition was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in reductio and construction arguments: adding to a balanced side produces predictable direction of inclination; supports proofs by removing or adding magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 3 (Subtracting from a balanced weight disturbs equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarly, if anything be taken away from one of the weights, they are not in equilibrium but incline towards the weight from which nothing was taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paired with Postulate 2 for reasoning about adjustments to achieve equilibrium; used in proofs by contradiction when assuming imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 4 (Coincidence of centres for equal similar planes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When equal and similar plane figures coincide if applied to one another, their centres of gravity similarly coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables transferring centre-of-gravity conclusions between congruent/similar pieces when applied or superposed; used in decompositions into equal parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 5 (Similarity preserves relative position of centres of gravity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In figures which are unequal but similar the centres of gravity will be similarly situated. By points similarly situated in relation to similar figures I mean points such that, if straight lines be drawn from them to the equal angles, they make equal angles with the corresponding sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to infer centres' positions in similar shapes via similarity mappings; important in scaling arguments and relating small and large similar components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 6 (Equality-preserving equilibrium under substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If magnitudes at certain distances be in equilibrium, (other) magnitudes equal to them will also be in equilibrium at the same distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows replacing a magnitude by an equal one without changing equilibrium — used in constructing commensurable decompositions for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 7 (Centre of gravity inside figures with uniformly concave perimeter)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any figure whose perimeter is concave in (one and) the same direction the centre of gravity must be within the figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A geometric constraint used to place centres of gravity internally; used implicitly in arguments about medians and intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. I (Book I) — Weights which balance at equal distances are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Weights which balance at equal distances are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by removing the difference and invoking Postulate 3; fundamental rule used repeatedly to deduce equality from equilibrium at equal arms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II — Unequal weights at equal distances incline to greater
rubrics_metrics.description: Unequal weights at equal distances will not balance but will incline towards the greater weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by taking away the difference to reduce to equal weights and applying Postulate 2; used to reason about direction of imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III — Unequal weights balance at reciprocally proportional distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Unequal weights will balance at unequal distances, the greater weight being at the lesser distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A and B balance about distances AC and BC respectively, then AC < BC when A > B; conversely if AC < BC then A > B. Proof by reductio using Postulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IV — Centre of gravity of two equal weights
rubrics_metrics.description: If two equal weights have not the same centre of gravity, the centre of gravity of both taken together is at the middle point of the line joining their centres of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Prop. 3 via reductio; used to combine equal parts and locate combined centres at midpoints of segment joining their individual centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V — Centre of gravity of three equal magnitudes on a line
rubrics_metrics.description: If three equal magnitudes have their centres of gravity on a straight line at equal distances, the centre of gravity of the system will coincide with that of the middle magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from Prop. IV; extended by corollaries to odd/even numbers of equally spaced equal magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries on symmetric collections of magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cor.1: For any odd number of magnitudes equally spaced with symmetric equalities, the system centre coincides with the middle one. Cor.2: For even numbers with symmetry conditions, the centre is the midpoint of the two middle ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to handle decompositions into many equal pieces (parallelograms, strips) and to deduce centres of composite figures by symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Props. VI & VII — Commensurable/incommensurable magnitudes balance reciprocally
rubrics_metrics.description: Two magnitudes, whether commensurable (Prop. 6) or incommensurable (Prop. 7), balance at distances reciprocally proportional to the magnitudes; proof via subdivision into equal parts (commensurable case) and approximation/reduction (incommensurable case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive method: break magnitudes into equal small parts to form equal-magnitude arrays on lever arms so that centre can be located at the point dividing the base in ratio DC:CE. For incommensurable, approximate by commensurable remainders and reason by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII — Centre of remainder after removing part
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be a magnitude whose centre of gravity is C, and AD a part of it whose centre of gravity is F, then the centre of gravity of the remaining part will be a point G on FC produced such that GC:CF = (AD):(DE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a formula for locating centre of remaining portion after subtracting a part; follows from equilibrium properties and is used in decomposition arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX — Centre of gravity of a parallelogram lies on middle-point joining line
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any parallelogram lies on the straight line joining the middle points of opposite sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by subdivision of the parallelogram into many equal small parallelograms and application of Postulate 4 and earlier propositions about equal spaced systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X — Centre of gravity of a parallelogram is intersection of diagonals
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a parallelogram is the point of intersection of its diagonals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Prop. IX; alternative proof uses that two equal triangles (split by a diagonal) have centres that superpose under a suitable application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XI — Centres correspond in similar triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: If abc and ABC are similar triangles and g, G points similarly situated, then g is centre of gravity of abc iff G is centre of gravity of ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by reductio: non-correspondence would contradict Postulate 5; used to transfer centroid conclusions under similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XII — Centre-line correspondence under similarity and midpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two similar triangles abc, ABC and d, D the midpoints of bc, BC respectively; if the centre of gravity of abc lies on ad, then that of ABC lies on AD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive similarity proof showing corresponding proportional segments and angles, hence corresponding centres lie on corresponding medians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIII — Centre of gravity lies on any median of a triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: In any triangle the centre of gravity lies on the straight line joining any angle to the middle point of the opposite side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by subdividing the triangle into many small parallelograms (or triangles) and using earlier propositions about centres of such pieces; alternative proof given via similarity and decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIV — Centroid is intersection of two medians
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any triangle is at the intersection of the lines drawn from any two angles to the middle points of the opposite sides respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary of Prop. XIII; establishes the classical centroid concurrency property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XV — Centre of gravity of a trapezium formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If AD, BC are parallel sides of a trapezium ABCD (AD smaller) bisected at K, F respectively, then the centre of gravity lies at G on EF such that GE:GF = (2·BC + AD) : (2·AD + BC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: extend sides to meet at O, locate centres of triangles OAD and OBC on certain lines, and use weighted-combination reasoning (Props. 6–8) with subdivisions of a diagonal to obtain ratio; used to compute centroid in trapezia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion via circumscribed/inscribed similar sectors (On Spirals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an area bounded by any arc of a spiral and the lines joining the extremities of the arc to the origin, it is possible to circumscribe about the area one figure, and to inscribe in it another figure, each consisting of similar sectors of circles, such that the circumscribed figure exceeds the inscribed by less than any assigned area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: bisect angle BOC repeatedly to produce arbitrarily small sector OCr; construct sequences of similar circular sectors meeting successive radii at spiral points; compare circumscribed and inscribed figures term-by-term to show difference < assigned bound (classical exhaustion). This is the key method for area results of spirals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 18 (tangent-perpendicular circumference relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: I. For A the end of first turn and OB perpendicular to OA meeting tangent at A at B, OB = circumference of the 'first circle'. II. For A' end of second turn OB' = 2 × circumference of second circle. III. Generally if A_n be end of nth turn and OB meets tangent at A_n in B_n then OB_n = n · (circumference of nth circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by contradiction: assume OB greater/less than claimed circumference, construct auxiliary lines meeting circles and spiral, derive impossible inequalities using arcs vs chords and previous propositions (Prop.7,14,15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 20 (perpendicular to radius meets tangent — arc equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is on the first turn and OT drawn perpendicular to OP meets the tangent at P in T', and K is intersection of initial line with circle of radius OP, then OT is equal to the arc KP measured in the 'forward' direction. Generally for P on nth turn, OT = (n−1)·p + arc KP (p = circumference of circle radius OP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: suppose OT greater/less than arc, construct chord/line meeting circle and spiral, use compositional inequalities and equal-radius relations (Props. 7,14,15) to contradict equalities like OQ = OP, hence deduce equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 21/22/29 (arbitrary small difference between circumscribed and inscribed)
rubrics_metrics.description: By repeatedly bisecting angle BOC and building circumscribed and inscribed figures from similar sectors, the difference between circumscribed and inscribed figures can be made less than any assigned area; thus the spiral-bounded area can be squeezed arbitrarily closely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlies Archimedes' application of exhaustion to spiral areas and supports existence/uniqueness of limit-area values; explicit construction given comparing corresponding sectors and noting equality/inequalities between forward/backward arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24 (area of first spiral turn = one-third first circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area bounded by the first turn of the spiral and the initial line is equal to one-third of the 'first circle' (i.e., R1 = (1/3)·C1). More generally, the area cut off by a radius OP in the first turn equals one-third of the sector of the circle of radius OP bounded by the initial line and OP (measured forward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assume inequality either way, circumscribe or inscribe similar-sector figures with area arbitrarily close to R1 and obtain contradictions via summation/proportionality of sector radii (using arithmetic progression of radii and Prop.10 Cor.1). Method extends to later turns by adding multiples of circle circumferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: General area formula for radius-vector sweeping (spiral)
rubrics_metrics.description: If OP is reached after n complete turns plus a fraction, the complete area described by the radius vector from the beginning up to position OP equals (1/3)·(n·C + sector KLP) (C = area of circle with radius OP); specialized forms given depending on n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by summing areas contributed by successive complete turns (each proportional to circles with radii forming arithmetic progression) and using the one-third relation for each sector/turn (extension of Prop. 24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 25/26 (general ratio for spiral arc area versus circular sector)
rubrics_metrics.description: If BC is any forward arc on any turn (not exceeding a complete turn), and if a circle with centre O and radius OC meets OB in B', then (area of spiral between OB and OC) : (sector OB'C) = {OC·OB + 4(OC − OB)^2} : OC^2 (general formula). Prop.25 is a special case giving specific numeric ratios (e.g. 7:12 for the second turn case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses circumscribed/inscribed similar-sector approximations, arithmetic progression properties of radii, and proportionality of sector areas to squares of radii; set up an auxiliary circle whose radius-square equals OC·OB + 4(OC−OB)^2 to compare areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 27 (ratios of ring-areas R1,R2,R3...)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R1 is area of first turn, R2 area added by second complete turn, R3 by third, etc., then R1:R2:R3:... are in the ratio 1:2:3:... (i.e., successive ring areas are proportional to 1,2,3,...). Various relations among cumulative sums and nth-circle areas are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Prop.26 applied to successive turns; uses algebraic manipulation of sector/circle areas and proportionality to radii-squares. Provides sequence structure for spiral ring areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 28 (ratio E:F for areas between spiral and differing circular arcs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given BC an arc forward on some turn, draw two circles (radius OB and OC) meeting the other radius in C' and B' respectively. Let E' be area bounded by larger circular arc B'C, line B'B, and spiral BC; F the area bounded by smaller arc BC', line CC' and spiral BC. Then E:F = {OB + 2(OC − OB)} : {OB + τ(OC − OB)} (final form derived in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof manipulates Prop.26 relations for the two sectors and eliminates the intermediate sector area o to obtain an explicit formula for the ratio E:F in terms of OB and OC; used to compare the 'outer' and 'inner' differences between spiral and circular sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book II Prop. I (parabolic segments — centre of gravity combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P,P' be two parabolic segments and D,E their centres of gravity respectively, the centre of gravity of the two segments taken together will be at a point C on DE determined by the relation given (text indicates proportional construction using equal-area rectangles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes suggests replacing parabolic segments by rectangles equal in area (possible due to prior quadrature results) to determine combined centre via earlier equilibrium propositions (Book I Props. 6,7).
